title: Structured Progressive Knowledge Activation for LLM-Driven Neural Architecture Search
claim: Isolating one functional factor per edit avoids entangled side effects, yielding far faster search and higher final accuracy than baselines.
layout: 2 stacked panels: top flow diagram contrasting holistic vs factor-scoped edits, bottom annotated scatter plot
description: The figure has two stacked panels. Panel (a) is a four-box diagram. At top left, an Architecture box shows PyTorch-style code with two lines tagged by blue and green Factor A and Factor B labels. A gray arrow labeled 'Holistic edits' leads down to a peach 'Functional Entanglement' box. That box shows LLM Searching with mixed-factor arrows between Factor A and Factor B, and a red X marking 'Unpredictable outcomes'. A curved arrow leads right to a 'Function-factor Tokens' box with Function, Operator, Action, Factor and patch tokens. From there, a 'Freeze other factor' arrow with a lock icon points down to 'Searching: Function → Patch'. That box has two steps, select function then generate patch tokens, and ends with a green check for 'Predictable outcomes'. Panel (b) is a plot of best-so-far accuracy against search iteration. A green 'Ours' curve rises steeply to 83.74. Baselines appear as colored stars. Red arrows mark '28.1× faster' and '+15.60 ACC'.
caption: Motivation for structure-guided editing in LLM-driven NAS. {(a)} Free-form edits entangle functional factors and often break interfaces, while factor-scoped tokens enable where-to-how edits to isolate the intervention target. {(b)} CLRS-DFS results show faster progress and higher OOD accuracy with fewer search iterations.
abstract: This paper focuses on a key challenge in Neural Architecture Search (NAS): integrating established architectural knowledge while exploring new designs under expensive evaluations. Large language models (LLMs) are a promising assistant for NAS because they can translate rich architectural and coding priors into executable code edits. However, in practice, seemingly local revisions often propagate into non-local behavioral and performance shifts because a single edit can inadvertently couple multiple interacting functional factors, a phenomenon we refer to as functional entanglement. To make LLM knowledge usable under such entanglement, we propose Structured Progressive Knowledge Activation (SPARK), which activates relevant priors by explicitly selecting the functional factor to modify and conditioning the edit on that factor. This factor-conditioned editing reduces entangled side effects and yields more targeted, reliable architecture modifications. On CLRS-DFS, SPARK achieves a 28.1x sample-efficient architecture evolution speedup and yields a 22.9\% relative improvement in OOD accuracy. Our code is available at https://github.com/AIM-ResearchLab/SPARK.
